In Czechia, the analytic results are based on a sample drawn to be representative of the population of 16-to-65-year-olds residing in the country at the time of data collection, with additional analyses to check that non-response does not introduce significant bias. The country notes do not report the specific sampling weight variable name(s) or any replicate-weight scheme, so the exact implementation details (e.g., whether W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT-style weights and BRR/jackknife were applied) are not documented in the provided text. For users of the underlying microdata, OECD/Survey of Adult Skills practice is to apply the provided complex-survey weights when estimating population-representative means, shares at proficiency levels, and regression associations; if replicate weights are available, they should be used for uncertainty estimates.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the Survey of Adult Skills 2023 Second Cycle sample for Czechia, consisting of 5057 adults aged 16-65 who participated in the survey (response rate 40%). Analyses are described as representative of the population of about 6.8 million 16-to-65-year-olds residing in Czechia, irrespective of nationality/citizenship/language status.

data.outcome_summary: The OECD Survey of Adult Skills 2023 country notes for Czechia summarize adult proficiency in three domains—literacy, numeracy, and adaptive problem solving—assessed in 2022-23 among adults aged 16-65. The assessment is administered exclusively on digital tablets and estimates proficiency on 500-point scales, with proficiency levels used to describe what adults can do. Czechia’s mean performance is close to the OECD average in literacy (260) and adaptive problem solving (250), and above average in numeracy (267). The notes report shares at low and high proficiency levels (e.g., literacy Level 1 or below: 25%; numeracy Level 1 or below: 21%; adaptive problem solving Level 1 or below: 29%) and describe how results vary by age, educational attainment, gender, and immigrant background. They also report associations between numeracy proficiency and labour force participation, unemployment risk, and wages, and between proficiency and well-being/civic engagement, while noting that doorstep respondents are excluded from some cross-cycle comparisons for comparability.
